READY

1. Verification begins by defining reversibility as a measurable contract before you touch the system, because an unreversible claim is just a guess until it is testable. Write down the exact end state that must be restored, including file paths, service states, and configuration values that must be identical before and after. For example, if you install nginx on Ubuntu 24.04, your contract states that after rollback the /etc/nginx directory must be absent, the www-data service listener on port 80 must be gone, and no nginx processes may remain in the process table.

2. Take a machine-readable baseline of the system before installing anything, so that you have a ground truth to compare against later rather than relying on memory. The baseline should capture installed packages, listening ports, running services, and checksums of configuration directories the software is likely to touch. For example, on a Fedora server, run `rpm -qa > baseline-packages.txt`, `ss -tlnp > baseline-ports.txt`, and `sha256sum /etc/hosts` to create snapshot files you can diff after rollback.

3. Verify the installation method itself is reversible by choosing a transactional package manager over a manual tarball extraction whenever possible. A package manager records the manifest of every file it writes, giving you an authoritative list to remove later, whereas a tarball leaves no such record. For example, installing htop with `apt install htop` records every path in dpkg's database, while extracting a htop tarball into /usr/local scatters files you must remember and find yourself.

4. Confirm after installation that the package manager's recorded manifest matches what actually landed on disk, because partial installs silently break rollback assumptions. Compare the list of files the package claims to own against a filesystem diff built from your pre-install snapshot. For example, after installing redis-server on Debian, run `dpkg -L redis-server` and diff that list against the delta from a find-based snapshot, verifying nothing appeared in /etc/redis beyond the documented redis.conf.

5. Verify that configuration files are written to predictable, documented locations rather than scattered across the system, because scattered configs are the most common source of rollback residue. Check that the software respects standard hierarchy paths, keeping system config in /etc and internal state in its designated data directory. For example, when installing Prometheus, confirm the main config sits in /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml and the TSDB lives in /var/lib/prometheus, exactly matching the paths declared in the package's post-install scripts.

6. Before modifying any configuration, save a copy of each file you will edit along with a checksum of its original state, so you can later prove it was restored byte-for-byte. This differs from an operational backup: here it is verification evidence, and it should record the timestamp and the exact command that produced it. For example, before editing /etc/ssh/sshd_config to add a Match block, run `cp -a` into /root/config-evidence/sshd_config.orig with `sha256sum` output, then after rollback diff the live file against the stored copy.

7. Enumerate every dependency the software pulls in and decide in advance which existed before your install and which are new, because rollback must not remove shared libraries that other software still needs. A dependency that predates your installation must survive your rollback untouched. For example, installing certbot on CentOS pulls python3-certbot as new while python3-openssl was already present for system tooling, so your rollback plan removes the former and explicitly protects the latter.

8. Verify that dependency versions are pinned in your install record, so that a rollback-and-reinstall test reproduces exactly the same dependency graph. Floating version references make reversibility unverifiable because the second install can silently resolve different library versions. For example, a requirements.txt entry of `requests==2.32.3` guarantees a reinstall after rollback lands on the same version, whereas a bare `requests` line could resolve to a different release the following week.

9. Record file and directory permissions before installation and again afterward, and put the expected permission state into your rollback criteria, because mode bits outside the package manifest can survive an uninstall. Pay special attention to world-writable paths and setuid bits that a service might create at runtime. For example, after installing a build agent that writes to /var/cache/buildagent, verify the directory is mode 0750 owned by the buildagent group, and that rollback deletes the directory entirely instead of leaving 0777 cache files behind.

10. Verify that the software runs under a dedicated service account created at install time, and that the account itself is part of the rollback checklist. A dedicated user isolates the software's file ownership so you can confidently locate every orphaned file by uid after removal. For example, installing Grafana creates a grafana system user, and a verified rollback should run `userdel grafana` and then confirm with `find / -user grafana` that no files remain owned by that account.

11. Test the service restart cycle explicitly: verify the software stops cleanly, its processes disappear, and its ports are released, because a zombie holding a port will poison every later test. Watch for daemons that respawn through socket activation or systemd timers after you believe they are stopped. For example, after installing an application served by apache2, run `systemctl stop apache2`, then verify with `ss -tlnp` that port 443 no longer appears and `ps` shows no remaining apache2 worker processes.

12. Verify that the software survives a full host reboot and that its startup mechanism is confined to one identifiable unit, so rollback has a single clean thing to disable. Startup hooks scattered across cron, rc.local, and shell profiles are nearly impossible to fully reverse. For example, a monitoring daemon that installs both /etc/systemd/system/monitor.service and an @reboot crontab entry requires removing both, which you discover only by rebooting the host and re-checking with `systemctl list-unit-files` and `crontab -l`.

13. Test interruption during installation in a disposable environment, because true reversibility means the system must also survive a half-finished install. The safest test is a virtual machine snapshot, a deliberately partial installation, and an attempt to clean up afterward. For example, in a throwaway VirtualBox VM, start `apt install postgresql-16`, kill the process mid-post-install-script, then verify that `dpkg --configure -a` repairs the package state and `apt remove --purge postgresql-16` returns the system to baseline.

14. Simulate a network interruption during installation, since downloads are the most common failure point and a cut fetch can leave partially unpacked archives in caches and temporary directories. The test should confirm that either the retry completes cleanly or the abort path deletes the partial artifacts. For example, install Ansible via pip inside a Docker container and use trickle to throttle then sever the download of the ansible-core wheel, verifying that pip's cache holds no half-written wheel that a later install would corrupt.

15. Take a system-level backup immediately before installation, in a form you have actually proven restorable, because an untested backup is a hope, not a guarantee. Exercise the restore on a separate machine or VM so that testing it does not destroy your live evidence. For example, before installing Docker Engine on a production-adjacent VM, create an LVM snapshot with `lvcreate --snapshot`, then restore that snapshot onto a second cloned disk in a spare VM to prove it boots with the pre-Docker package list.

16. Back up configuration directories separately from the full system snapshot, because config rollback often needs finer granularity than a whole-disk restore can offer. A per-file backup with a checksum manifest lets you restore one config file without clobbering other deliberate changes. For example, before editing an nginx sites-available file to add a reverse proxy block for the new app, copy it to a timestamped tar archive under /var/backups/installs/ with a sha256 manifest, so rollback restores just that file via `tar --extract` without touching an unrelated TLS change made that week.

17. Verify that the installation separates program files from user data by design, because reversibility breaks down the moment rollback must decide whether a file belongs to the application or the user. Check the install manifest against the filesystem hierarchy to ensure data lives in /var/lib or the documented data directory, never beside binaries. For example, when installing Gitea from its release package, confirm configuration lives in /var/lib/gitea/custom and repositories in /var/lib/gitea/data while the binary sits in /usr/local/bin, so a rollback that removes only manifest files provably leaves user repositories untouched.

18. Prove with a live test that the installation does not modify user data outside its declared footprint, by seeding canary files and verifying they are unchanged. Create a marker file in a home directory and a dummy database row, then check byte-identity after the install-configure-rollback cycle. For example, before installing the Nextcloud server package, create ~/canary.txt containing the string leopard-42 with a recorded checksum, and after the full cycle confirm the file still reads leopard-42 with an unchanged modification time, proving the installer never wandered into the home directory.

19. Verify the rollback through the same mechanism used for installation first, because the package manager's own removal path is the shortest and most auditable reversal. A purge removal is stronger than a plain removal, since it also deletes configuration files the package created. For example, rolling back an installed jq via `apt purge jq` passes verification only if `dpkg -l jq` shows the package as deinstalled with no config-files row and `which jq` returns nothing.

20. Verify snapshot-level rollback as a second, independent path, because some installations modify state outside the package database and only an image restore catches those. Test the restore in the same virtual machine by installing over the snapshot and then reverting the disk. For example, on a Proxmox host, snapshot VM 101 before installing fail2ban, install it, revert the snapshot, and verify that `apt list --installed` no longer mentions fail2ban and /etc/fail2ban is gone, proving the hypervisor-level safety net works.

21. After rollback, hunt for leftover files that neither the package manager nor the snapshot caught by diffing the post-rollback filesystem against the pre-install baseline. Common residue includes logs, runtime directories, and caches created on first run rather than at install time. For example, after removing the filebeat shipper, a diff between baseline and current find output reveals /var/lib/filebeat/registry still exists because the running agent created it after installation, so the rollback procedure must be amended to delete that path explicitly.

22. Verify that service state and integration points are restored after rollback, including disabled units, removed firewall rules, and unregistered cron jobs. Package files can be gone while their integrations persist and silently expose or destabilize the system. For example, after rolling back a VPN client install that had added a ufw rule allowing UDP 51820, verify with `ufw status numbered` that the rule is absent, and confirm `systemctl is-enabled` on the client's unit returns a not-found error rather than enabled.

23. Run the entire cycle end-to-end once in a clean test environment — baseline, install, configure, restart, rollback, diff — and accept nothing less than an empty diff against the baseline as passing. A full-cycle run matters because individual reversibility checks can each pass while their combination leaks something. For example, on a Vagrant machine defined by a fresh Vagrantfile, script the cycle and run it three times consecutively, confirming the post-rollback diff against baseline is empty every time, proving the procedure does not depend on leftover state from a previous run.

24. Document the verified procedure as an executable runbook, so reversibility becomes a repeatable property of the system rather than the memory of one person. The runbook should contain the exact baseline commands, install commands, verification diffs, and rollback commands, each annotated with the output that counts as passing. For example, commit a rollback.sh into the deployment repository that recreates the checksum baseline, installs vault from HashiCorp's apt repository, and after removal asserts vault is absent, then run it in CI on every release so the guarantee is continuously re-verified instead of assumed.
